summary: Specifies delivering IPv4 multicast services to IPv4 clients over an IPv6 multicast network with stateless IPv4-in-IPv6 encapsulation, useful for DS-Lite customers.

plainLanguage.summary: Carrying old-style group broadcasts inside new-style envelopes.

questions: how to deliver ipv4 multicast over ipv6
subtitle: How an IPv6-only network can deliver IPv4 multicast streams, such as IPTV, by wrapping them in IPv6 multicast.

tldr.problem: In a Dual-Stack Lite (DS-Lite) network, IPv4 multicast would have to be copied into one unicast tunnel per subscriber, wasting IPv6 network bandwidth and overloading the AFTR.
tldr.mechanism: A multicast AFTR (mAFTR) wraps each IPv4 multicast packet in an IPv6 multicast packet whose addresses embed the IPv4 ones, and a multicast B4 (mB4) in the customer's device joins the IPv6 tree and unwraps the packets. The address mapping is stateless.
tldr.outcome: The IPv6 network replicates the traffic natively, close to the receivers. It is a Proposed Standard, not limited to DS-Lite, and has not been obsoleted.

facts.label: Embedded IPv4 address
facts.value: last 32 bits of the IPv6 address

facts.label: Fragmentation
facts.value: oversized packet split into two IPv6 packets by the mAFTR

today: RFC 8114 is a Proposed Standard, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. Its companion RFC 8115 defines a DHCPv6 option for provisioning the prefixes it uses.

sections.title: The Multicast Problem in DS-Lite
sections.content:
DS-Lite (RFC 6333) lets operators share public IPv4 addresses while giving users only IPv6. IPv4 packets travel in IPv4-in-IPv6 tunnels between the customer's B4 and the operator's AFTR (Address Family Transition Router), and RFC 6333 covers unicast only.

If IPv4 multicast were used through this setup, the AFTR would have to process every IGMP Report forwarded into the tunnels and copy the multicast packets into each tunnel. The RFC lists two consequences. First, the IPv6 network cannot replicate the data close to the receivers, so downstream bandwidth is consumed by sending multicast data over what is effectively unicast. Second, the AFTR spends significant resources on replication and may be overloaded.

The solution was developed with DS-Lite in mind but is generic. It can also apply to other contexts such as RFC 7596 and RFC 7597. It supports both Source-Specific Multicast (SSM) and Any-Source Multicast (ASM), though RFC 4607 recommends SSM where possible and it simplifies operation, for example by removing Rendezvous Point placement concerns.
sections.plainLanguage: Sending the same TV show separately to every house wastes the road. It would be better to send one copy and let the road split it near the houses.

sections.title: Scope
sections.content:
The RFC covers only IPv4 receivers that subscribe to IPv4 multicast groups and receive IPv4-formatted content over an IPv6-only, multicast-enabled network. Hosts behind the mB4 are assumed to be receivers only; a receiver that is also an IPv4 multicast source is not covered. A host with a built-in mB4 function is covered.

Appendix A gives IPTV as the use case. Most current IPTV content is likely to remain IPv4-formatted and outside the control of network providers, and many legacy receivers such as IPv4-only set-top boxes cannot be upgraded easily, so IPv4 service continuity must be guaranteed during the transition.
sections.plainLanguage: This only covers watching, not broadcasting. A person at home can receive the show but cannot start one for others.

sections.title: Solution Overview
sections.content:
Two new functional elements appear. The mB4 (Multicast Basic Bridging BroadBand) translates IGMP messages from IPv4 receivers into MLD messages for the IPv6 network and decapsulates the multicast packets it gets back. The mAFTR (Multicast AFTR) sits between the IPv4 multicast network and the IPv6 multicast network, encapsulates IPv4 multicast packets into IPv6 multicast packets, and acts as the IPv6 multicast source for them. The encapsulation is one-way, from the mAFTR to the mB4.

A subscription works like this. The IPv4 receiver sends an IGMP Report to the mB4. The mB4 builds the IPv6 group address (G6) from the IPv4 group address (G4) and, for source-specific reports, an IPv6 source address (S6) from the IPv4 source (S4), and sends an MLD Report. The PIMv6 Designated Router turns that into a PIMv6 Join, (*,G6) in ASM or (S6,G6) in SSM. The mAFTR receives the Join, extracts G4 (and S4), and sends the matching PIMv4 Join into the IPv4 network. The result is a tree with an IPv4 part upstream of the mAFTR and an IPv6 part downstream.

The mAFTR advertises the route to the uPrefix64 prefix in the IPv6 IGP, so IPv6 routers can run the Reverse Path Forwarding (RPF) check on the traffic. IPv6 routers treat the encapsulated packets as ordinary IPv6 multicast and forward on the outer header. For simplicity, the RFC recommends configuring the mAFTR as the RP for the IPv4-embedded IPv6 groups it manages.
sections.plainLanguage: The box at home asks for a show on behalf of the TV. The box at the other end fetches the show, puts it in a new-style envelope and sends it down the road once. The home box opens the envelope and hands the show to the TV.

sections.title: IPv4/IPv6 Address Mapping
sections.content:
Two prefixes are provisioned to the mAFTR and every mB4, and both sides MUST use the same ones and the same algorithm. mPrefix64 is a /96 IPv6 multicast prefix, of an ASM or SSM flavor, and MUST come from the IPv6 multicast address space. uPrefix64 is an IPv6 unicast prefix, either the Well-Known Prefix 64:ff9b::/96 or a Network-Specific Prefix, used to build source addresses as in RFC 6052.

The algorithm is simple: concatenate the 96 bits of mPrefix64 with the 32 bits of the IPv4 group address. To go back, take the last 32 bits. Because the IPv4 address sits in the last 32 bits, dotted decimal notation can be used when writing it. The prefixes can be configured by an out-of-band mechanism, manually, or with a provisioning protocol such as DHCPv6 (RFC 8115).
sections.plainLanguage: The new address is just a fixed street name with the old house number attached at the end, so anyone who knows the street name can turn it back into the old address.

sections.title: How the mB4 and mAFTR Behave
sections.content:
mB4. It combines IGMP/MLD proxying (RFC 4605) with address synthesis. Upstream it acts as an MLD host; downstream it acts as an IGMP router. When it receives an IPv6 multicast packet whose group is in mPrefix64 and whose source is in uPrefix64, it decapsulates it (RFC 2473) and forwards the IPv4 packet normally; otherwise it MUST silently drop the packet. Encapsulation shrinks the effective MTU by an IPv6 header, so the mAFTR MUST fragment an oversized result into two IPv6 packets and the mB4 MUST reassemble them.

mAFTR. It MUST be the multicast source whose address comes from uPrefix64 and MUST advertise a route to uPrefix64 in the IPv6 IGP. It keeps separate IPv4 and IPv6 Tree Information Bases (TIB4 and TIB6) bridged by an IPv4-in-IPv6 virtual interface, and interworks PIM Join/Prune messages: a (*,G6) or (S6,G6) Join becomes a (*,G4) or (S4,G4) Join. On the first IPv4 packet it may send an explicit (S4,G4) Join to the source and switch from the shared tree to the shortest path tree. Whether the RPF check is done on the second lookup is left to the implementation.

Scope. If several mPrefix64s exist with distinct scopes, the mB4 MUST pick the one whose scope matches the IPv4 group so the IPv6 scope does not exceed the IPv4 scope. If none matches and the mB4 must preserve scope, the mapping SHOULD fail. The mB4 MAY be configured not to preserve scope.
sections.plainLanguage: The home box opens envelopes only if they carry the right street name, and throws away any others. The far-end box wraps the show in envelopes and passes along requests from the home boxes.

sections.title: Deployment Options
sections.content:
Several variations are described. The mAFTR can be co-located with the IPv6 DR and MLD Querier, so it handles MLD Reports directly and sends PIMv4 Joins. If it is co-located with the IPv4 DR next to the original source, it can build the IPv6 packets directly and PIMv4 Joins become unnecessary. Several nodes can run the mAFTR function for robustness and load sharing, as long as they use the same prefixes and algorithm. An mAFTR may also be configured with a list of IPv4 groups and sources, and silently drops flows outside it.

In static mode the mAFTR permanently instantiates (S6,G6) and (*,G6) entries from a pre-configured (S4,G4) list, which suits conveying all streams in the core while only popular ones go into the access network. In dynamic mode entries are created or withdrawn when PIMv6 messages arrive.

Appendix B covers version mismatches between IGMP and MLD: the mB4 should perform the router portion of the IGMP version matching the MLD version in use (IGMPv2 for MLDv1, IGMPv3 for MLDv2). IPv4 SSM requires MLDv2 in the IPv6 network.
sections.plainLanguage: Operators can put the wrapping box in different places. They can keep it always sending popular shows or only send a show when someone asks for it.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC says it adds no new security concerns beyond those in Section 5 of RFC 6052, Section 10 of RFC 3810 and Section 6 of RFC 7761. It also states that, unlike solutions that map IPv4 multicast flows to IPv6 unicast flows, it does not exacerbate Denial-of-Service attacks.

An mB4 SHOULD get configuration that lets it preserve the multicast scope when mapping addresses in either direction. A CPE with the mB4 function SHOULD accept incoming MLD messages and traffic for groups its local receivers have joined. The RFC makes no IANA requests.
sections.plainLanguage: It does not open new doors for bad guys. The home box should keep the right door open for the shows its family asked for.
